questions.q: Which description best defines true labor?
ch: Irregular contractions that produce no cervical change over several hours
Regular uterine contractions causing progressive cervical effacement and dilation with fetal descent
Rupture of membranes with pooling of alkaline fluid but no contractions at all
Bloody show alone in the absence of any measurable cervical dilation
Painful contractions relieved entirely by hydration and a change of position
questions.exp: Labor is regular uterine contractions causing progressive cervical effacement and dilation plus fetal descent; Braxton-Hicks contractions are irregular and produce no cervical change.
why: Irregular contractions without cervical change are Braxton-Hicks contractions, not labor.
Rupture of membranes may precede labor, but without contractions producing cervical change it is not labor.
Bloody show is a common sign of impending labor, but labor requires demonstrated cervical change.
Contractions that resolve with hydration and repositioning suggest false labor rather than true labor.

questions.q: The third stage of labor is best defined as which interval?
ch: The first one to two hours postpartum while hemostasis is established
Onset of regular contractions to the beginning of the active phase at 6 cm
Onset of labor to complete cervical dilation at 10 cm
Complete cervical dilation to delivery of the baby
Delivery of the baby to delivery of the placenta
questions.exp: The third stage runs from delivery of the baby to delivery of the placenta; the first stage is onset to full 10 cm dilation, the second stage is full dilation to delivery of the baby, and the fourth stage is the first 1-2 hours postpartum.
why: The first 1-2 hours postpartum, when hemostasis is established, is the functional fourth stage.
That describes the latent portion of the first stage, before the active phase begins at 6 cm.
Onset of labor to full 10 cm dilation is the first stage.
Full dilation to delivery of the baby is the second stage.

questions.q: Per ACOG and the Consortium on Safe Labor, the active phase of the first stage is now generally considered to begin at what cervical dilation?
ch: 6 cm dilation
3 cm dilation
4 cm dilation
8 cm dilation
10 cm dilation
questions.exp: The active phase is now defined as beginning at 6 cm rather than the older Friedman threshold; this ACOG and Consortium on Safe Labor change reduced unnecessary primary cesarean delivery.
why: 3 cm is below any accepted active-phase threshold and would label most latent labor as active.
4 cm was the older Friedman threshold that the 6 cm definition replaced.
8 cm is well into active labor; using it would delay recognition of the active phase.
10 cm is complete dilation, which marks the end of the first stage rather than the start of the active phase.

questions.q: Which findings confirm rupture of membranes at the bedside?
ch: Nitrazine paper turning yellow together with absent ferning on microscopy
Bloody show accompanied by cervical dilation of about 4 cm
A globular firm uterus with lengthening of the umbilical cord
Turtle sign with retraction of the fetal head against the perineum
Pooling of fluid, nitrazine turning blue, and ferning on microscopy
questions.exp: Rupture of membranes is confirmed by pooling of fluid, nitrazine paper turning blue because amniotic fluid is alkaline, and ferning on microscopy; AmniSure/PAMG-1 is added when the result is uncertain.
why: Nitrazine turns blue, not yellow, with alkaline amniotic fluid, and ferning should be present.
Bloody show and cervical dilation reflect labor progress but say nothing about membrane status.
A globular firm uterus with cord lengthening indicates placental separation in the third stage.
The turtle sign indicates shoulder dystocia, not rupture of membranes.

questions.q: Immediately after spontaneous rupture of membranes, what is the nurse's first priority?
ch: Encourage ambulation and oral hydration to promote descent
Perform a digital cervical exam to document dilation and station
Increase the oxytocin infusion to augment contraction strength
Assess the fetal heart rate for evidence of cord prolapse
Send amniotic fluid for nitrazine and ferning confirmation
questions.exp: After rupture of membranes the nurse immediately assesses the fetal heart rate because cord prolapse causes fetal bradycardia; fluid color (meconium), amount, and odor are then noted.
why: Ambulation and hydration are appropriate in early labor but not before fetal heart rate assessment.
A cervical exam may follow, but it does not detect the fetal bradycardia of cord prolapse.
Raising oxytocin before assessing the fetal heart rate risks worsening an unrecognized problem.
Nitrazine and ferning confirm a rupture that has already occurred; they are not the immediate safety priority.

questions.q: Late decelerations on the fetal monitor are mechanistically explained by which process?
ch: Maternal fever with chorioamnionitis
Fetal movement producing accelerations
Uteroplacental insufficiency
Fetal head compression
Umbilical cord compression
questions.exp: Late decelerations reflect uteroplacental insufficiency and are the worrisome pattern; early decelerations come from head compression and variable decelerations from cord compression.
why: Maternal fever is not the mechanism given for late decelerations.
Accelerations with fetal movement are a reassuring finding, not a deceleration.
Head compression produces early decelerations, which are benign.
Cord compression produces variable decelerations rather than late ones.

questions.q: A postpartum patient with asthma and chronic hypertension has continued hemorrhage despite oxytocin. Which additional agent is safest?
ch: Misoprostol given simultaneously with a high-dose oxytocin infusion
Tranexamic acid, given within 3 hours of the onset of bleeding
Magnesium sulfate, to relax the uterus and slow the rate of bleeding
Carboprost, because prostaglandin F2-alpha is first line for uterine atony
Methylergonovine, because ergot agents act fastest on the uterine muscle
questions.exp: Tranexamic acid, most effective when given within 3 hours of bleeding onset, is the appropriate additional agent here because carboprost is contraindicated in asthma and methylergonovine in hypertension.
why: Prostaglandins should not be given simultaneously with oxytocin, and this choice ignores both contraindications.
Magnesium sulfate relaxes the uterus and would worsen atonic bleeding; it is used for seizure prophylaxis and fetal neuroprotection.
Carboprost (PGF2-alpha) is contraindicated in asthma.
Methylergonovine is contraindicated in hypertension.

questions.q: Which criteria must be met before diagnosing arrest of the first stage of labor?
ch: At 6 cm or more, no cervical change for at least 4 hours with adequate contractions of 200 MVU or more
Failure to deliver after 1 hour of pushing in a nulliparous patient with an epidural
Any Category II tracing persisting through two consecutive cervical examinations
A Bishop score below 5 after 12 hours of prostaglandin cervical ripening
No cervical change for 2 hours at 4 cm regardless of contraction adequacy
questions.exp: First-stage arrest requires the patient to be at 6 cm or more with no cervical change for at least 4 hours despite adequate contractions of 200 MVU or more, or at least 6 hours with inadequate contractions.
why: Pushing duration applies to arrest of descent in the second stage, where 3 hours for a nullipara plus 1 hour for an epidural is allowed.
A Category II tracing prompts intrauterine resuscitation, not a diagnosis of labor arrest.
The Bishop score quantifies cervical favorability for induction; it is not an arrest criterion.
The 4 cm and 2 hour standard reflects the older Friedman thresholds that the 6 cm definition replaced.

questions.q: During the third stage, which combination of findings indicates that the placenta has separated?
ch: Sustained tachysystole with more than five contractions in ten minutes
Loss of deep tendon reflexes with a decreasing respiratory rate
Cord shortening with a soft, wide, ill-defined uterine fundus
A gush of blood, lengthening of the cord, and a globular firm uterus
A boggy uterus with heavy lochia and maternal tachycardia
questions.exp: Signs of placental separation are a gush of blood, lengthening of the cord, and a uterus that becomes globular and firm; the cord should never be pulled.
why: Tachysystole is an oxytocin complication, not a sign of placental separation.
Loss of deep tendon reflexes with respiratory depression indicates magnesium toxicity.
The cord lengthens and the uterus becomes firm and globular; these findings are the reverse.
A boggy uterus with heavy lochia suggests uterine atony and postpartum hemorrhage.

questions.q: The fetal head delivers then retracts tightly against the perineum, and the shoulders do not deliver with routine traction. What is the correct response?
ch: Apply firm fundal pressure to push the anterior shoulder past the symphysis
Elevate the presenting part and proceed directly to emergent cesarean delivery
Call for help and begin the HELPERR maneuver sequence, avoiding fundal pressure
Start a magnesium sulfate infusion to relax the uterus and free the shoulder
Increase the oxytocin infusion to strengthen contractions and drive expulsion
questions.exp: The turtle sign signals shoulder dystocia, an obstetric emergency: call for help and work through the HELPERR sequence, and do NOT apply fundal pressure.
why: Fundal pressure is explicitly contraindicated in shoulder dystocia and further impacts the shoulder.
Elevating the presenting part and moving to cesarean is the response to cord prolapse, not to a dystocia after the head has delivered.
Magnesium sulfate is used for seizure prophylaxis and fetal neuroprotection, not for shoulder dystocia.
More oxytocin increases contraction force against an impacted shoulder and risks injury.

questions.q: Which pathogen is the most common cause of bronchiolitis?
ch: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV)
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
Adenovirus, an occasional cause
Rhinovirus, another viral cause
Parainfluenza virus, types 1 and 3
questions.exp: RSV, respiratory syncytial virus, is the most common cause of bronchiolitis and the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the US; rhinovirus, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza, influenza, and adenovirus also cause it.
why: Human metapneumovirus does cause bronchiolitis, but far less often than RSV.
Adenovirus is an occasional cause and is not the leading one.
Rhinovirus is listed among the other agents, not as the most common cause.
Parainfluenza is the classic cause of croup and only a minor cause of bronchiolitis.

questions.q: Bronchiolitis primarily affects which group, and when does it peak?
ch: Infants under 2 years, peaking at 12-18 months of age
Neonates in the first two weeks of life, with no seasonal variation
Infants under 2 years, peaking at 3-6 months, in winter and early spring
Children 6 months to 3 years, peaking in fall and early winter
School-age children and adolescents, peaking in the late spring months
questions.exp: Bronchiolitis primarily affects infants under 2 years, peaks at 3-6 months of age, and has winter and early-spring seasonality.
why: The peak is at 3-6 months, considerably younger than 12-18 months.
Bronchiolitis is not a disease of the first two weeks of life and it is strongly seasonal.
Ages 6 months to 3 years with a fall and early-winter peak describes croup.
School-age children and adolescents who wheeze are far more likely to have asthma than bronchiolitis.

questions.q: Which statement about the diagnostic workup of bronchiolitis is correct?
ch: Serial complete blood counts are used to grade the severity of illness
A chest X-ray should be obtained routinely to confirm the diagnosis
The diagnosis is clinical, and routine chest X-ray and labs are not recommended
RSV PCR is required in every infant before any treatment can be started
A normal pulse oximetry reading excludes the diagnosis of bronchiolitis
questions.exp: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis; routine chest X-ray is not recommended because it shows nonspecific hyperinflation or atelectasis and drives unnecessary antibiotics, and routine labs are not needed.
why: Severity is graded by work of breathing, feeding ability, hydration, apnea, and SpO2, not by serial blood counts.
Routine chest X-ray is specifically not recommended because it is nonspecific and drives unnecessary antibiotics.
RSV PCR or antigen testing is done only when it changes management, such as cohorting or ruling out influenza.
Pulse oximetry guides admission decisions, but a normal saturation does not exclude bronchiolitis.

questions.q: Which examination findings are the hallmark of bronchiolitis?
ch: Diffuse wheezes and fine crackles with tachypnea and retractions
A barking, seal-like cough with inspiratory stridor and hoarseness
Focal consolidation with dullness to percussion and a high fever
An absent cough with drooling and a tripod sitting posture
Clear lungs with normal work of breathing and an isolated fever
questions.exp: The hallmark findings are diffuse wheezes and fine crackles with tachypnea, nasal flaring, retractions, prolonged expiration, and often hypoxia, following a URI prodrome.
why: A barking cough with inspiratory stridor describes croup rather than bronchiolitis.
Focal consolidation with high fever points to pneumonia.
Absent cough with drooling and tripod posture suggests epiglottitis.
Clear lungs with normal work of breathing is inconsistent with bronchiolitis.

questions.q: Why does a trial of albuterol usually fail in an infant with bronchiolitis?
ch: Because concurrent systemic steroids are required for albuterol to have any effect
Because infants cannot generate enough inspiratory flow to inhale a nebulized drug
Because beta-2 receptors are absent from the airway until about 2 years of age
Because the wheeze in bronchiolitis is transmitted from the upper airway only
Because the obstruction is mucus plugging and edema, not reversible bronchospasm
questions.exp: Bronchiolar obstruction comes from epithelial necrosis, edema, and mucus plugs creating a ball-valve effect with air trapping, not from reversible smooth-muscle bronchospasm, which is why bronchodilators are not routinely recommended.
why: Systemic steroids are also not routinely recommended, so adding them would not rescue albuterol.
Nebulized delivery does work in infants; the problem is the nature of the obstruction, not drug delivery.
Beta-2 receptors are present in infancy, and receptor absence is not the explanation given.
The wheeze arises from the inflamed lower airways, the bronchioles, not from transmitted upper-airway noise.

questions.q: An infant with bronchiolitis has moderate-to-severe distress and hypoxia not met by low-flow oxygen. Which escalation is recommended?
ch: Empiric intravenous antibiotics pending a chest X-ray result
Chest physiotherapy with postural drainage every four hours
Nebulized hypertonic saline given in the emergency department
Heated high-flow nasal cannula, escalating to CPAP or ICU if it fails
Nebulized albuterol every 20 minutes plus a systemic corticosteroid
questions.exp: Heated high-flow nasal cannula is used for moderate-severe distress or hypoxia not met by low-flow oxygen; it provides humidified flow and some PEEP, and failure warrants escalation to CPAP or the ICU.
why: Antibiotics are not routinely recommended, and routine chest X-ray is what drives exactly this unnecessary treatment.
Chest physiotherapy is among the therapies that are not routinely recommended.
Hypertonic saline may modestly reduce length of stay in admitted patients but is not recommended in the ED setting.
Bronchodilators and systemic steroids are not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis.

questions.q: Which nursing intervention best addresses the primary airway problem in bronchiolitis?
ch: Nasal suctioning before feeds and as needed, with the head elevated
Restricting oral fluids to reduce the production of secretions
Obtaining a daily chest X-ray to follow atelectasis and hyperinflation
Administering a scheduled bronchodilator before each feeding
Placing the infant flat and supine to promote chest expansion
questions.exp: Prioritizing a patent airway means nasal bulb or nasopharyngeal suctioning before feeds and as needed with the head elevated; suctioning and hydration do more than any drug because the problem is airway plugging.
why: Hydration must be maintained with small frequent feeds or IV/NG fluids if tachypnea impairs safe oral intake.
Routine chest X-ray is not recommended and would do nothing for the airway.
Bronchodilators are not routinely recommended and do not clear the mucus plugging that causes the obstruction.
The infant should be positioned with the head elevated rather than flat and supine.

questions.q: A 6-week-old former premature infant with bronchiolitis is described by parents as unusually quiet. Which concern is highest?
ch: Reactive airway disease that will respond to a bronchodilator trial
Simple tiredness from the URI prodrome, expected around day 3-5
Post-tussive emesis causing a self-limited aversion to feeding
Apnea, which can be the presenting sign in young or premature infants
Bacterial superinfection requiring immediate empiric antibiotic therapy
questions.exp: Apnea can be the first sign of bronchiolitis in young or premature infants, so a quiet baby is not reassuring; apnea with pallor or cyanosis is a red flag, especially under 2 months.
why: Bronchodilator-responsive reactive airway disease is a feature of asthma in an older child.
The illness does peak around day 3-5, but a quiet young infant must be evaluated for apnea rather than assumed to be tired.
Feeding difficulty matters, but it does not carry the immediate risk that apnea does.
Antibiotics are not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis and would not explain the quiet infant.

questions.q: Which agent is given as a single dose to infants entering or during their first RSV season?
ch: Nebulized hypertonic saline 3% used prophylactically
Oral dexamethasone at the onset of the RSV season
Heated high-flow nasal cannula started at the first cough
Palivizumab, dosed monthly through the season
Nirsevimab, a long-acting RSV monoclonal antibody
questions.exp: Nirsevimab is a long-acting monoclonal antibody given as a single dose for infants entering or during the first RSV season; it is passive immunization and largely replaces palivizumab.
why: Hypertonic saline is a treatment that may shorten stay in admitted patients; it is not prophylaxis.
Systemic steroids are not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis and have no preventive role.
High-flow nasal cannula is an escalation therapy for distress, not an immunization.
Palivizumab is given monthly to select high-risk infants, not as a single dose for most infants.

questions.q: Which factor most strongly favors admitting an infant with bronchiolitis?
ch: Diffuse wheezing that has not changed after nebulized albuterol
Age under 12 weeks together with hypoxia, dehydration, or apnea
Hyperinflation and atelectasis reported on a chest X-ray
A cough lingering for 10 days in an infant who is feeding normally
A positive RSV swab in a well-appearing, well-feeding infant
questions.exp: Disposition drivers are age under 12 weeks, prematurity, comorbidities, hypoxia, dehydration, apnea, and severe work of breathing; pulse oximetry and feeding ability guide the admission decision.
why: Bronchodilators usually fail in bronchiolitis, so a non-response is expected and not a disposition criterion.
Chest X-ray is not recommended, and hyperinflation with atelectasis is a nonspecific finding.
Parents are taught that cough lingers 2-3 weeks, so a lingering cough with normal feeding is expected.
RSV testing is done only when it changes management, and a positive swab in a well infant does not.

questions.q: Which triad is classic for croup?
ch: Expiratory grunting with focal consolidation and dullness to percussion
Wheezing with fine crackles and preceding rhinorrhea in an infant
Drooling with high fever and a toxic appearance and no cough
Sudden choking with unilateral decreased breath sounds and no prodrome
Barking, seal-like cough with inspiratory stridor and hoarseness
questions.exp: The classic croup triad is a barking, seal-like cough with inspiratory stridor and hoarseness, usually preceded by 1-3 days of URI or coryza with low-grade fever.
why: Grunting with focal consolidation points to pneumonia rather than upper-airway obstruction.
Wheezing with fine crackles in an infant describes bronchiolitis.
Drooling, high fever, and a toxic child with no cough suggest epiglottitis.
Sudden onset with no viral prodrome suggests an inhaled foreign body.

questions.q: Which virus most commonly causes croup?
ch: Influenza virus during flu season
Measles virus, now rarely seen
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
Parainfluenza virus, types 1 and 3
Adenovirus, an occasional cause
questions.exp: Parainfluenza virus, types 1 and 3, is the classic and most common cause of croup; RSV, influenza, adenovirus, and rarely measles can also cause it.
why: Influenza can cause croup but is not the classic culprit.
Measles is a rare cause, especially where vaccination is widespread.
RSV can cause croup but is best known as the leading cause of bronchiolitis.
Adenovirus is listed as a less common cause of croup.

questions.q: Why does a few millimeters of subglottic edema produce stridor in a toddler?
ch: Because the subglottis is the narrowest point and resistance rises steeply as the radius falls
Because the trachea has no cartilage and collapses inward on inspiration
Because bronchiolar mucus plugging creates a ball-valve air-trapping effect
Because vocal cord paralysis accompanies the viral inflammatory response
Because alveolar surfactant is depleted by the viral infection at this age
questions.exp: The subglottis is the narrowest part of a young child's airway and is encircled by rigid cricoid cartilage, so by Poiseuille's law resistance rises with the inverse fourth power of the radius and small edema causes disproportionate obstruction.
why: The subglottic ring is rigid cricoid cartilage, which is precisely why edema there is so consequential.
Ball-valve mucus plugging in the bronchioles is the mechanism of bronchiolitis.
Hoarseness comes from laryngeal inflammation, not from vocal cord paralysis.
Surfactant depletion is not part of the croup mechanism described.

questions.q: A toddler has mild croup with a barking cough and no stridor at rest. What treatment is indicated?
ch: Nebulized epinephrine now, with discharge after a brief recovery
A single dose of dexamethasone, given even for mild disease
A five-day course of oral amoxicillin for a presumed bacterial cause
Scheduled nebulized albuterol every four hours until symptoms resolve
No medication; supportive humidified air and reassurance alone
questions.exp: Dexamethasone is first-line for ALL severities of croup, even mild disease; a single PO, IM, or IV dose of roughly 0.15-0.6 mg/kg has a long half-life that covers the illness and reduces return visits.
why: Nebulized epinephrine is reserved for moderate-to-severe croup with stridor at rest and requires 3-4 hours of observation.
Croup is viral, so antibiotics have no role in treatment.
Albuterol treats lower-airway bronchospasm and does not relieve subglottic edema.
Steroids benefit even mild croup, reducing symptom duration, return visits, and admissions.

questions.q: After nebulized epinephrine is given for croup, what must happen before discharge?
ch: A repeat AP neck film to confirm the steeple sign has cleared
A second dose of nebulized epinephrine given exactly one hour later
Admission for at least 24 hours of continuous pulse oximetry
Documentation of a Westley score of zero before the child may leave
Observation for 3-4 hours to detect rebound stridor
questions.exp: Nebulized epinephrine acts fast but its effect wanes in about 2 hours, so the child must be observed 3-4 hours for rebound stridor before discharge.
why: The steeple sign is nonspecific and imaging is not required in croup at all.
A scheduled second dose is not required; the child is observed and re-dosed only if needed.
Most children are managed as outpatients after an adequate observation period.
The Westley score guides severity and disposition, but a score of zero is not a discharge requirement.

questions.q: Which tool grades croup severity to guide disposition?
ch: The Bishop score, using cervical dilation, effacement, station, consistency, and position
The Westley score, using stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and consciousness
The Braden scale, using sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, and nutrition
The Parkland formula, using body weight and percentage of total body surface area
The NPIAP staging system, using the anatomic depth of tissue involvement
questions.exp: The Westley Croup Score grades severity using stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and level of consciousness, and it guides the disposition decision.
why: The Bishop score quantifies cervical favorability for labor induction.
The Braden scale scores the risk of developing a pressure injury.
The Parkland formula calculates fluid resuscitation volume in burns.
NPIAP staging describes the anatomic depth of a pressure injury.

questions.q: A child arrives toxic-appearing, drooling, sitting in a tripod position with high fever and no cough. What does this suggest?
ch: Classic croup that simply presents at the severe end of the spectrum
Spasmodic croup, the recurrent allergic variant with nighttime onset
An inhaled foreign body with sudden onset and no viral prodrome
Epiglottitis — do not agitate the child and secure the airway
Bronchiolitis with impending respiratory failure and a silent chest
questions.exp: Drooling, a toxic appearance, tripod posture, and an absent cough suggest epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis rather than croup; do not agitate the child, and secure the airway.
why: Croup produces a barking cough, and the child is not toxic-appearing or drooling.
Spasmodic croup has sudden nighttime onset without a viral prodrome and is not toxic.
A foreign body is sudden in onset but does not produce fever, drooling, and toxicity.
Bronchiolitis is a lower-airway disease of infants with wheeze and crackles, not drooling with stridor.

questions.q: Which nursing action is most important while a child with croup is being evaluated?
ch: Insert an intravenous line immediately so steroids can be given by vein
Draw a complete blood count and blood culture before any treatment
Keep the child calm on the caregiver's lap and minimize invasive exams
Obtain an AP neck radiograph promptly to look for the steeple sign
Place the child supine on the stretcher for a careful oropharyngeal exam
questions.exp: Agitation worsens airway obstruction, so the child is kept calm in a position of comfort on the caregiver's lap while invasive exams and crying are minimized.
why: Oral dexamethasone is as effective as IM, so an IV stick is an unnecessary upset in a distressed child.
Croup is a clinical diagnosis; routine labs are not needed and a needle stick only agitates the child.
Imaging is not required, and the trip to radiology agitates the child for a nonspecific finding.
Laying the child supine and probing the oropharynx increases distress and can worsen obstruction.

questions.q: A child with croup is vomiting and cannot keep down oral dexamethasone. What is the appropriate alternative?
ch: Nebulized budesonide as an alternative or adjunct steroid
Oral prednisone for five days once the vomiting settles
Withhold steroids entirely and treat with humidified oxygen only
Nebulized epinephrine used as a substitute for the steroid dose
Oral antipyretics alone, on the basis that they reduce airway swelling
questions.exp: Nebulized budesonide is the alternative or adjunct steroid when oral dosing is not tolerated because of vomiting; it is more costly, so dexamethasone is generally preferred and simpler when it can be given.
why: Croup is treated with a single long-acting dexamethasone dose, not a five-day prednisone course.
Every croup patient should receive a steroid, so withholding it is not appropriate.
Nebulized epinephrine does not alter the disease course and must always be paired with a steroid.
Antipyretics are supportive only and do not treat airway edema.

questions.q: A child with croup received dexamethasone and nebulized epinephrine but is now quiet, with decreasing air entry and lethargy. How should this be read?
ch: Expected improvement, since the nebulized epinephrine has taken effect
Rebound stridor, which resolves on its own without further treatment
A critical warning of impending airway failure requiring escalation
Normal night-time worsening that will improve with cool humid air
Simple exhaustion from crying, best managed by letting the child sleep
questions.exp: A fatiguing, quiet child with decreasing air entry and lethargy, or a poor response to epinephrine and steroids, is a critical warning of impending airway failure requiring emergent escalation and possible intubation.
why: Improvement would show less stridor with good air entry and an alert child, not lethargy.
Rebound stridor requires re-treatment and continued observation, and it does not cause lethargy.
Symptoms are characteristically worse at night, but altered mental status and falling air entry are never attributed to that.
Lethargy with decreasing air entry signals respiratory failure, not tiredness from crying.

questions.q: Which finding defines a Stage 1 pressure injury?
ch: A wound base obscured by slough or eschar so depth is unknown
Erythema that whitens completely when light pressure is applied
Intact skin with non-blanchable erythema over a bony prominence
Partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis and a shallow open ulcer
Full-thickness loss with visible subcutaneous fat in the wound bed
questions.exp: Stage 1 is intact skin with non-blanchable erythema; if the redness blanches (whitens) with pressure it is not yet a pressure injury.
why: A base obscured by slough or eschar describes an unstageable injury.
Erythema that blanches with pressure is not a pressure injury at all.
Partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis is Stage 2.
Full-thickness loss with visible subcutaneous fat is Stage 3.

questions.q: A sacral wound exposes tendon and bone and has undermining at its edges. How is it staged?
ch: Deep tissue injury, because the wound extends deeply
Stage 2, because the dermis is exposed
Stage 3, because subcutaneous fat is visible
Stage 4, because fascia, muscle, tendon, or bone is exposed
Unstageable, because undermining is present
questions.exp: Stage 4 is full-thickness loss that exposes fascia, muscle, tendon, or bone, and it may have undermining and tunneling.
why: Deep tissue injury is intact or blistered skin with persistent deep discoloration, not an open wound exposing bone.
Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis, not exposed bone.
Stage 3 shows subcutaneous fat with no exposed fascia, muscle, tendon, or bone.
Unstageable means the base is obscured by slough or eschar; here the base is visible.

questions.q: How should a Braden Scale score be interpreted?
ch: It measures wound surface area in order to track healing over time
A lower score indicates higher risk, with 18 or below considered at risk
It predicts the need for surgical flap closure of Stage 3-4 wounds
A higher score indicates higher risk, with 18 or above considered at risk
It stages wound depth once a pressure injury has already developed
questions.exp: The Braden Scale scores sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction/shear; think of it as a golf score, where a lower number means higher risk, with 18 or below flagged as at-risk.
why: Braden is a risk-prediction score, not a wound measurement tool.
Braden does not predict the need for surgical flap closure.
The direction is reversed: a lower Braden number, not a higher one, means higher risk.
Staging uses the NPIAP system based on anatomic depth, not the Braden Scale.

questions.q: Unrelieved pressure over a bony prominence causes ischemia once it exceeds which threshold?
ch: The interface pressure of about 100 mmHg
The systolic blood pressure of about 120 mmHg
The mean arterial pressure of about 65 mmHg
The capillary closing pressure of about 32 mmHg
The central venous pressure of about 8 mmHg
questions.exp: Capillary closing pressure is roughly 32 mmHg; interface pressures above this over time cause local ischemia, reperfusion injury, and cell death, and hypotension, vasopressors, and anemia lower the tolerable threshold further.
why: Interface pressure is what is applied to the skin; the threshold it must exceed is capillary closing pressure.
Systolic blood pressure is not the pressure at which skin capillaries close.
Mean arterial pressure is a systemic perfusion measure, not the local capillary threshold.
Central venous pressure reflects volume status rather than tissue interface loading.

questions.q: Which set of nursing measures correctly prevents pressure injuries?
ch: Turn every 4 hours, use a donut cushion, and massage reddened bony areas
Keep the head of bed above 45 degrees and slide the patient up in bed
Place a ring cushion under the sacrum and rest the heels on the mattress
Reposition only when the patient reports discomfort over a bony prominence
Turn q2h with a 30-degree lateral tilt, float the heels, and lift rather than drag
questions.exp: Reposition at-risk patients at least every 2 hours using a 30-degree lateral tilt, keep the head of bed at or below 30 degrees to limit shear, float the heels off the mattress, and lift rather than drag the patient.
why: Donut and ring cushions are not used, massage over bony prominences worsens deep injury, and turns are every 2 hours.
The head of bed should be at or below 30 degrees, and sliding the patient up in bed creates shear.
Ring cushions are avoided, and the heels must be floated off the mattress rather than resting on it.
Many at-risk patients have sensory impairment and will never report discomfort, so turning is scheduled.

questions.q: A bedbound patient with poor perfusion has stable, dry, intact eschar on the heel. What is the correct action?
ch: Leave the eschar intact and offload the heel from the mattress
Apply an alginate dressing to absorb drainage from beneath it
Start systemic antibiotics for presumed underlying osteomyelitis
Sharply debride the eschar so the wound can be staged
Apply collagenase daily until the eschar has fully dissolved
questions.exp: Stable, dry, intact eschar on an ischemic heel acts as a biologic cover and should not be debrided; instead the heel is floated off the mattress to remove the load.
why: Alginate is for highly exudative or cavity wounds and has no role on dry intact eschar.
Antibiotics are reserved for spreading cellulitis, sepsis, or biopsy-proven osteomyelitis.
Sharp debridement of stable heel eschar removes the natural cover and can worsen the wound.
Enzymatic debridement with collagenase is still debridement and is avoided for stable dry heel eschar.

questions.q: A Stage 4 sacral wound has granulated in and is now shallow. How should it be documented?
ch: As a Stage 2, because the current depth reaches only the dermis
As a Stage 1, because the wound surface is nearly intact again
As unstageable, because the original depth can no longer be seen
As a deep tissue injury, because damage began at the muscle-bone interface
As a healing Stage 4, because pressure injuries are never reverse-staged
questions.exp: Staging reflects anatomic depth at its worst, not a healing timeline; pressure injuries heal with granulation and scar rather than regenerating lost tissue layers, so a healing Stage 4 is documented as a healing Stage 4.
why: Reverse-staging a healing wound down to Stage 2 is exactly the documentation error to avoid.
A closing surface does not return the wound to Stage 1, because lost tissue layers are not regenerated.
Unstageable applies when slough or eschar obscures the base, not to a granulating wound.
Deep tissue injury describes intact discolored skin or a blood-filled blister, not a healing open wound.

questions.q: A persistent maroon-purple area of intact skin over the heel does not blanch. What is it, and why does it matter?
ch: An unstageable wound whose base is obscured by adherent slough
Deep tissue injury, which can rapidly declare as a Stage 3 or 4 wound
A Stage 1 injury, which resolves with a single episode of repositioning
Moisture-associated skin damage from incontinence and maceration
A resolving bruise that needs only observation over several days
questions.exp: Persistent non-blanchable deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration or a blood-filled blister is a deep tissue injury; damage starts at the muscle-bone interface and evolves outward, so a small purple area can deteriorate fast despite an intact surface.
why: Unstageable requires an open wound with slough or eschar obscuring the base; here the skin is intact.
Stage 1 is non-blanchable erythema rather than deep maroon or purple discoloration, and it does not carry the same rapid-deterioration risk.
Moisture-associated skin damage arises from incontinence and maceration in skin folds, not as deep discoloration over a bony prominence.
This discoloration is persistent and non-blanchable, which is what distinguishes it from a simple bruise.

questions.q: A non-healing full-thickness sacral wound probes to bone. What is the appropriate workup?
ch: MRI with bone biopsy and culture to evaluate for osteomyelitis
Serial photography with weekly reassessment of the Braden score
Negative pressure wound therapy started before any imaging is done
Albumin and prealbumin levels alone to explain the poor healing
Superficial wound swab culture followed by empiric oral antibiotics
questions.exp: A persistent non-healing full-thickness wound over bone warrants MRI with bone biopsy and culture to evaluate for osteomyelitis, rather than a superficial swab.
why: Photography and Braden reassessment are useful monitoring but will not diagnose bone infection.
Negative pressure wound therapy is contraindicated over untreated osteomyelitis, so the infection must be evaluated first.
Nutritional markers support the healing assessment but do not evaluate the bone.
Superficial swab cultures are unreliable; colonization is not infection and should not be treated in a stable wound.

questions.q: A hospitalized patient develops a new Stage 3 pressure injury. Which statement best captures its significance?
ch: It should be reverse-staged as it heals to demonstrate quality improvement
It confirms that malnutrition alone was the cause of the wound
It is a hospital-acquired CMS never event demanding immediate escalation
It requires systemic antibiotics because all Stage 3 wounds are infected
It is an expected complication of critical illness and needs no escalation
questions.exp: A new full-thickness Stage 3 or 4 wound in a hospitalized patient is a hospital-acquired CMS never event that is not reimbursed and demands immediate escalation; prevention is framed by the SSKIN bundle.
why: Pressure injuries are never reverse-staged as they heal.
Malnutrition is one driver, but immobility, shear, moisture, perfusion, and age all contribute.
Antibiotics are indicated only for spreading cellulitis, sepsis, or biopsy-proven osteomyelitis.
Pressure injuries are described as largely preventable and a key marker of care quality, not an accepted complication.

questions.q: A burn is leathery, dry, and insensate. What depth does this describe?
ch: Superficial (first-degree), involving the epidermis only
Partial-thickness (second-degree), extending into the dermis
Superficial burn with blistering and marked moist pain
Fourth-degree burn, which by definition reaches muscle and bone
Full-thickness (third-degree), extending through the dermis
questions.exp: Full-thickness (third-degree) burns extend through the dermis and appear leathery, dry, and insensate because the nerve endings have been destroyed.
why: Superficial first-degree burns are red and painful with no blisters and involve the epidermis only.
Partial-thickness second-degree burns are moist, blistered, and very painful.
Blistering with moist painful skin is partial-thickness; superficial burns do not blister.
Fourth-degree burns reach muscle or bone, beyond what this description states.

questions.q: Using the Rule of Nines in an adult, the entire front torso represents what proportion of TBSA?
questions.exp: By the Rule of Nines the front torso is 18% and the back is 18%; the head is 9%, each arm 9%, each anterior or posterior leg 9%, and the perineum 1%.
why: 9% is the head, an arm, or one anterior or posterior leg surface, not the whole front torso.
1% is the perineum, and also the size of the patient's palm.
36% is the front torso and back combined, not the anterior torso alone.
4.5% would be half of a 9% segment rather than a torso surface.

questions.q: An 80 kg adult has 30% TBSA of partial-thickness and full-thickness burns. By the Parkland formula, how much lactated Ringer's is given in the first 8 hours from the time of injury?
questions.exp: Parkland is 4 mL x weight in kg x %TBSA of lactated Ringer's over 24 hours, so 4 x 80 x 30 = 9,600 mL total, with half of it, 4,800 mL, in the first 8 hours from the time of injury.
why: 9,600 mL is the full 24-hour Parkland volume; only half of it goes in the first 8 hours.
2,400 mL is a quarter of the 24-hour volume and under-resuscitates the first 8 hours.
1,200 mL results from using 4 mL per kilogram without multiplying by the %TBSA.
19,200 mL is double the 24-hour requirement and is the kind of over-resuscitation that causes fluid creep.

questions.q: Which statement about estimating TBSA for burn resuscitation is correct?
ch: Superficial first-degree burns are included in the TBSA calculation
The Rule of Nines is the preferred estimation method in children
The patient's whole hand including fingers equals about 5% TBSA
Superficial first-degree burns are NOT counted in the TBSA calculation
TBSA is unnecessary once fluids are titrated to hourly urine output
questions.exp: Superficial first-degree burns are excluded from the TBSA used in the Parkland calculation; the Rule of Nines applies to adults, the Lund-Browder chart is used in children, and the patient's palm is about 1% TBSA.
why: First-degree burns are explicitly excluded from the TBSA used for Parkland.
The Lund-Browder chart is used in children; the Rule of Nines applies to adults.
The patient's palm is about 1% TBSA, not 5%.
Urine output titration guides ongoing therapy, but TBSA is still needed to start the resuscitation.

questions.q: A patient rescued from a closed-space house fire is confused, and the pulse oximeter reads 99%. What does this most likely indicate?
ch: Rhabdomyolysis from deep muscle damage after an electrical burn
Adequate oxygenation, so hypoxia can be excluded as a cause
Possible carbon monoxide poisoning, since pulse oximetry cannot detect it
Early burn shock from capillary leak in the first 24 hours
Mafenide-induced metabolic acidosis affecting mental status
questions.exp: Pulse oximetry is falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning because it cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin, so a normal SpO2 after a closed-space fire does not rule it out; obtain co-oximetry and give 100% oxygen.
why: Rhabdomyolysis follows electrical injury with dark urine and rising CK, not a closed-space fire exposure.
A normal pulse oximetry reading does not exclude hypoxia when carboxyhemoglobin is present.
Burn shock causes hypovolemia and hypotension, not isolated confusion with a normal saturation right after rescue.
Mafenide acidosis is a complication of topical therapy applied later, not of the initial rescue.

questions.q: What is the primary endpoint used to titrate fluid resuscitation in an adult with major burns?
ch: Normalization of the carboxyhemoglobin level on repeat co-oximetry
Resolution of pain at the burn site during dressing changes
A normal chest X-ray obtained six hours after the injury
Urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/h measured hourly via a Foley catheter
Strict adherence to the calculated Parkland volume regardless of response
questions.exp: Resuscitation is titrated to urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults, about 1 mL/kg/h in children, monitored hourly via Foley, rather than to the formula alone.
why: Carboxyhemoglobin guides oxygen therapy for CO poisoning, not the fluid rate.
Pain control matters, but full-thickness burns are painless and pain is not a perfusion endpoint.
The chest X-ray is often normal early and does not reflect resuscitation adequacy.
Blindly following the formula causes over-resuscitation, or fluid creep, with edema and compartment syndrome.

questions.q: A patient with a circumferential full-thickness burn of the forearm loses distal pulses and reports paresthesia. What does this require?
ch: Immediate silver sulfadiazine application with elevation of the limb
An increase in the opioid dose with reassessment in four hours
Reduction of the fluid rate to limit further extremity swelling
Application of mafenide acetate so that it penetrates the eschar
Urgent escharotomy to relieve the constricting burn eschar
questions.exp: Circumferential full-thickness burns can restrict perfusion or ventilation; loss of pulses or paresthesia distal to the burn must be reported and may need urgent escharotomy.
why: Topical antimicrobials and elevation do nothing to relieve a constricting circumferential eschar.
Increasing analgesia masks the ischemia instead of treating it, and delay costs the limb.
Under-resuscitating a burn patient to control swelling causes shock and does not restore the pulse.
Mafenide penetrates eschar for infection control but does not release the constriction.

questions.q: Which patient should NOT receive topical silver sulfadiazine?
ch: An adult with a partial-thickness burn of the anterior thigh
An infant under 2 months old with a documented sulfa allergy
An adult with a full-thickness burn needing a topical antimicrobial
A patient with a thigh burn who has already had tetanus prophylaxis
A patient with a leg burn who is receiving intravenous opioids
questions.exp: Silver sulfadiazine is avoided on the face and in sulfa allergy, G6PD deficiency, pregnancy near term, and infants under 2 months; it can also cause transient leukopenia.
why: Partial-thickness burns of the trunk or limbs are exactly where silver sulfadiazine is used.
Silver sulfadiazine is indicated as a topical antimicrobial for partial-thickness and full-thickness burn wounds.
Tetanus prophylaxis is given to every burn patient and does not preclude silver sulfadiazine.
Intravenous opioid analgesia is expected in burn care and is not a contraindication to the topical agent.

questions.q: Which finding by itself meets American Burn Association criteria for transfer to a burn center?
ch: A partial-thickness burn involving the hands, face, or genitalia
Any burn in an adult who reports pain during dressing changes
A 5% TBSA partial-thickness burn of the thigh in a healthy adult
A first-degree sunburn covering the back and both shoulders
A small blister on the forearm that healed without any dressing
questions.exp: ABA transfer criteria include partial-thickness burns over 10% TBSA, burns of the face, hands, feet, genitalia, or major joints, full-thickness burns, electrical and chemical injury, inhalation injury, and burns in the very young or old or with comorbidities.
why: Pain is universal in burn care and is not itself a transfer criterion.
A 5% partial-thickness burn is below the 10% TBSA threshold and is not in a special-site area.
First-degree burns are not even counted in TBSA and do not trigger transfer.
A small blister that has already healed requires no transfer.

questions.q: How does the pathophysiology of a major burn evolve after the first 48 hours?
ch: The wound becomes sterile as the eschar seals the skin barrier
It shifts to a hypermetabolic catabolic state with high infection risk
Metabolic demand falls, so calorie and protein needs decline sharply
Pain resolves once the full-thickness areas have become insensate
Capillary leak intensifies, so fluid rates must be steadily increased
questions.exp: The first 24-48 hours are dominated by capillary leak and burn shock; later phases shift to a hypermetabolic, catabolic state with high infection risk, the leading cause of late death, which is why high-protein high-calorie nutrition and early excision and grafting matter.
why: Loss of the skin barrier makes infection the leading cause of late death; eschar does not sterilize the wound.
Metabolic demand rises, which is exactly why high-protein, high-calorie nutrition is emphasized.
Full-thickness centers are insensate, but the surrounding partial-thickness areas remain very painful.
Capillary leak dominates the first 24-48 hours, and pushing fluids past that point causes fluid creep and compartment syndrome.
